subject: RLA
title: Claims vs. Evidence — Step by Step
tipLine: Same skill, broken into smaller steps this time — no timer, no pressure.

vocabTerms.definition: the belief or position a writer wants you to accept
the fact, example, or data offered to prove the claim

blocks.heading: Try this way of sorting it
blocks.body: Ask two questions, in order. First: "What does this sentence want me to believe?" — that's a candidate claim. Second: "Does this sentence prove something, or does it get proven?" — if it proves something, it's evidence. The claim is always the position; the evidence is always what's offered to back that position up.

blocks.heading: Worked example
blocks.body: "Community gardens should get city funding — the three that opened last year each cut nearby grocery costs by 15%." Claim: gardens should get funding (this is the belief being pushed). Evidence: the 15% cost drop (this is what proves it). Notice the claim is an opinion someone could disagree with; the evidence is a fact that argues for it.

blocks.question: "Public libraries should extend evening hours — three branches that tried it saw a 25% jump in visits." What's the claim?
blocks.feedbackCorrect: That's it — libraries extending hours is the belief being argued; the visit jump is what backs it up.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: Close — that one's evidence again. Try the two-question test: does it prove something, or get proven?
